findings.title: Water supply coverage in Gulu municipality
findings.summary: Gulu's water supply system covers the municipality and peri-urban areas but meets only about one third of total water demand.

findings.title: Groundwater characteristics in Uganda
findings.summary: Most boreholes in Uganda tap groundwater from weathered and fractured basement aquifers, with depths mostly less than 80 m and yields varying widely.

findings.title: Water contamination risks in Gulu District
findings.summary: Contamination of drinking water in Gulu can cause acute water-borne diseases such as cholera, dysentery, and typhoid.

findings.title: Gulu clean water supply project launched
findings.summary: A 2.1 billion shilling project was launched in 2025 to expand safe drinking water supply and protect natural water sources in Gulu City.

findings.title: Water sources status in Gulu District (2010)
findings.summary: A 2010 report details operational status and accessibility of water sources in Gulu District.

findings.title: Permeability of weathered bedrock aquifers in Uganda
findings.summary: Most boreholes in Uganda are deeper than 50 m with average depth around 70 m; transmissivity varies significantly with depth category.

findings.title: Predictors of water point sustainability in Gulu
findings.summary: Water source technology types and contamination risk scores predict sustainability and water quality of nonpiped water sources in Gulu.

findings.title: Gulu Water Supply and Sanitation Project
findings.summary: Construction started on a water supply and sanitation project serving over 341,000 people in Gulu and surrounding areas, drawing water from the Nile at Karuma.

findings.title: WASH assessment in Gulu District
findings.summary: A 2022 WASH assessment identified severe water shortages in Gulu District, especially in Paico and Bungatila sub-counties.

findings.title: Uganda borehole and transmissivity dataset
findings.summary: A digital dataset includes over 655 borehole records with metadata and pumping test data across Uganda including Gulu.

findings.title: Water contamination and flooding in Gulu City
findings.summary: Flooding during rainy seasons contaminates water sources in Gulu City, causing challenges in water quality and supply.

findings.title: Karuma-Gulu water project construction
findings.summary: Construction began in 2022 on the Karuma-Gulu water project including treatment plant and pipelines to Gulu city and peri-urban towns.

findings.title: Household water source and collection in Northern Uganda
findings.summary: Most households collect drinking water from protected sources but water quantity is below minimum standards and collection times are high.

findings.title: Water point failure case study in Uganda
findings.summary: Most water points in studied districts are deep boreholes (40-60 m) tapping weathered regolith and fractured bedrock aquifers with groundwater levels 1-5 m below ground.

findings.title: Catchment vulnerability in Gulu City
findings.summary: Gulu City lies in catchments vulnerable to dry spells; recent climate change has dried key water sources and micro-catchment degradation is worsened by human activities.

findings.title: Rehabilitation of war-time piped water schemes in Gulu
findings.summary: Gulu district plans to rehabilitate six abandoned piped water schemes originally built for displaced persons during the LRA insurgency.

population.methodLabel: 435 people inside the 1,000 m service circle per WorldPop Global per-country 2020, 100 m (University of Southampton, CC BY 4.0), projected 6 years to 2026 at 2.7–4.8%/yr (World Bank World Development Indicators (2025)). Range adds a ±20% band (Mayim screening assumption).
limitations: WorldPop's latest global year is 2020; growth since then is projected with the national rate, not observed.
WorldPop is a modelled distribution of census totals, not a count; the unconstrained model can place people on unbuilt land.
100 m grid cells on the edge of the service circle are approximated.
Everyone inside the service radius is assumed to be able and willing to walk to the point; terrain, land tenure and social barriers are not modelled.
The mapped-building estimate (3,903–5,947) differs by 8.6×; treat the two as bounds until a household count is done.

worldpop.source: WorldPop Global per-country 2020, 100 m (University of Southampton, CC BY 4.0)

alternative.methodLabel: 31 mapped buildings within 1000 m, scaled by 30.0x because OpenStreetMap returned more footprints than the analysis retains, at 4.2-6.4 people per building (Demo planning assumption).

recommendation.label: Solar-powered borehole with storage and tap stands
rationale: Drilled beside the road for rig access; groundwater evidence 0.43.
Chosen from 98 projects simulated household by household: $164 per person served over 10 years, the lowest among options that held in at least 70% of futures.
Serves 400 people in the design case (400 within a 30-minute round trip) and saves 259 hours of water collection a day; held in 24 of 24 ten-year futures.

components.name: Borehole
components.detail: Drilled, cased and gravel-packed borehole in the 60-95 m depth band implied by the groundwater evidence score. Actual depth is known only after drilling.

components.name: Solar pumping
components.detail: 700 Wp PV array, controller and submersible pump against an assumed 78 m pumping head.

components.name: Storage
components.detail: 9,000 L tank, sized at 1 day(s) of demand for 470 people at 20 L/person/day.

components.name: Distribution
components.detail: 460 m of conceptual distribution pipeline feeding 2 tap stand(s).

components.name: Monitoring
components.detail: Flow and system-status sensors with remote reporting for post-handover verification.

cost.accessMultiplierReason: Site is 118 m from the nearest mapped road on flat terrain — 1% mobilisation and logistics surcharge applied.
assumptions: Order-of-magnitude planning ranges for pre-feasibility screening — not a quotation, tender price or bill of quantities.
Quantities are sized for approximately 470 people at the service level assumed by the upstream sizing step.
Access surcharge applied to the subtotal: x1.01. Site is 118 m from the nearest mapped road on flat terrain — 1% mobilisation and logistics surcharge applied.
Totals are rounded outward to the nearest $1,000 (low down, high up) to avoid implying precision the method does not have.
Excludes land acquisition, taxes and import duties, permitting fees, contingency, and all recurrent operation and maintenance costs.
All unit rates are taken unchanged from the project coefficient table (RWSN/UNICEF rural water supply cost benchmarking (planning range)).
Drilling priced against the "moderate" depth band (60-95 m), selected by a groundwater evidence score of 0.43. Actual depth is only known after drilling.
Solar array rated at 700 Wp; no diesel or grid backup is priced.

output.formula: sustainable pump rate 1,800-2,567 L/h x effective pumping hours (5.731 kWh/m2/day x 0.78 = 4.47 h) x operational efficiency 0.82 = 6,600-9,410 L/day
caveats: Desk-study planning figures only. Borehole yield in particular is not guaranteed by a desk study: the sustainable rate must be confirmed by a step-drawdown and constant-rate pumping test on the completed borehole.
People supported assumes 20 L/person/day (WHO/UNICEF JMP service-level guidance); real consumption varies with walking distance, queueing time and the alternatives available.
